newsitem.title: USA: U.S. yet to make up its mind on Bosnia elections.
newsitem.headline: U.S. yet to make up its mind on Bosnia elections.

text.p: The United States has not yet decided whether to recommend delaying municipal elections in Bosnia, which Bosnian Serb leaders have threatened to boycott, Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Monday.
Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum, who is currently in Sarajevo, is discussing "precisely that" with international officials, Christopher told reporters.

"It is true that some of the parties, particularly the Bosnian Serbs...(have) brought forward obstacles to the going forward of the elections, but we have not reached a recommendation on that subject," he said.

Technically the decision rests with Robert Frowick, head of the organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission in Bosnia. But U.S. views are likely to weigh heavily with Frowick, a former State Department official.
The New York Times on Monday quoted U.S. officials as saying the Clinton administration had concluded that the elections, set for Nov. 23-24 should be put off.

The elections are viewed as the last chance for Bosnia to be reunited after a war that divided the country into ethnic ghettoes. But the Serbs have said they will not take part, citing security problems in villages in Serb territory resettled by Moslem refugees.

Christopher, speaking before talks with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko, said there was no question of the international peace force IFOR, whose mandate expires Dec. 20, extending its stay in Bosnia, as some Western diplomats have suggested.
Washington and its allies have yet to decide, however, on whether to replace IFOR with a smaller international force.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said it was "a possibility" that Frowick might postpone the elections. But he said Washington was waiting to see the outcome of Kornblum's talks before deciding its view.
